title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text:
This thesis asks whether the timing of review sessions changes how much new vocabulary adults still remember two months later. Sixty adult beginners learned the same two hundred words of Portuguese over four weeks. Half reviewed on an expanding schedule, with gaps that grew from one day to nine days. The other half reviewed the same number of times, but in massed sessions on consecutive days. At the end of the four weeks both groups scored almost identically. Eight weeks after that, the expanding group recalled roughly a third more words.

The difference was largest for abstract words and smallest for concrete nouns that could be pictured. Participants in the massed group rated their own learning higher throughout, which suggests that the feeling of fluency during study is a poor guide to what will last. The findings support building spaced schedules into self study tools by default, rather than leaving the timing to learners.

This work is a synthetic example written for the Chunkie project. The participants, data and references are invented.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text: Most adults who start a new language give up within a year, and the most common reason they give is that words do not stick. They learn a list on Monday, feel confident on Tuesday, and find on the following Monday that half of it has gone. Teachers tend to respond by assigning more practice. This thesis starts from a different question: whether the same amount of practice, arranged differently in time, would be enough.
embed_text:
1 Introduction
Most adults who start a new language give up within a year, and the most common reason they give is that words do not stick. They learn a list on Monday, feel confident on Tuesday, and find on the following Monday that half of it has gone. Teachers tend to respond by assigning more practice. This thesis starts from a different question: whether the same amount of practice, arranged differently in time, would be enough.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text:
Forgetting is not random. It is fastest shortly after learning and slows over time, so a word reviewed one hour after first meeting it gains little, because it had barely begun to fade. A word reviewed after it has partly faded, but before it is lost, is strengthened far more by the same effort. Schedules built on this idea space reviews further apart each time a word is recalled successfully.

Commercial flashcard applications have used such schedules for decades, yet classroom courses rarely do. Homework is set weekly, tests are announced in advance, and learners revise the night before. That pattern produces good test results and poor long term memory, and it is the pattern most adult learners have been trained in since school.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text:
The advantage of spread out practice over concentrated practice is among the most replicated findings in the study of memory. It appears for word lists, for facts, for motor skills and for mathematical procedures, in children and in older adults. The size of the benefit grows with the delay before the final test. On a test the next day, massed practice often looks just as good, and occasionally better.

That last detail matters for teaching. Any evaluation that tests learners soon after study will tend to favour cramming, and most classroom assessment does exactly that. A method can therefore look effective in every short evaluation and still leave learners with little a few months later.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text: Earlier studies disagree on whether the gaps between reviews should grow or stay the same. Some found expanding gaps clearly better. Others found uniform gaps just as good, provided the first gap was not too long. A plausible explanation is that expanding gaps help most when the first review comes early enough for recall to succeed, since a failed recall attempt teaches less than a successful one.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text: Learners are consistently poor at predicting what they will remember. When a word was seen a moment ago, it comes to mind easily, and that ease is mistaken for durable knowledge. Spaced review feels harder, because each review arrives after some forgetting, and so learners tend to judge it less effective even when it is working. If this holds for vocabulary, it would explain why learners who are free to choose rarely choose to space.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text:
Sixty adults between twenty two and sixty one years old took part, recruited through notices at two community centres. None had studied Portuguese or any other Romance language beyond a few holiday phrases. They were assigned at random to the expanding group or the massed group, thirty in each, and the groups did not differ in age, years of education or prior language study.

Four people left before the delayed test, two from each group, for reasons unrelated to the study such as moving away. The analysis uses the remaining fifty six.

chunk_text: The two hundred words were drawn from a frequency list of spoken Portuguese and split evenly into concrete words, such as kitchen objects and animals, and abstract words, such as feelings and ideas. Each word was shown with its English translation and a recorded pronunciation. Concrete words also had a simple line drawing, because pictures are the usual way such words are taught.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text:
Both groups met the new words in the same four introductory sessions in the first week. After that, each group completed twelve review sessions of twenty minutes over the remaining three weeks. The only difference was when those sessions happened. The expanding group reviewed after one, two, four, six and nine day gaps, while the massed group completed their reviews in blocks on consecutive days.

At the end of every review session, participants rated on a scale from one to seven how many of the words they expected to remember in two months. Recall was tested at the end of the four weeks and again eight weeks later. In both tests participants saw the English word and typed the Portuguese one, with minor spelling errors accepted.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text: Both groups remembered concrete words better than abstract ones at every point. The advantage of spacing, however, was concentrated in the abstract words. For concrete nouns, the two groups ended within a few words of each other. For abstract words, the expanding group recalled nearly twice as many. The pictures seem to have given concrete words a second route into memory that made the schedule matter less.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text: The massed group predicted better long term recall than the expanding group in every one of the twelve review sessions. Across all participants, a higher rating went with a slightly lower delayed score, not a higher one.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text: The pattern fits the view that effortful recall is what strengthens memory. Each expanding review arrived after some forgetting, so recalling the word took work, and that work paid off at the delayed test. The massed reviews arrived while the words were still fresh. They felt productive and cost little effort, which is exactly why they added little.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text: The most practical finding is the one in section 4.4. If learners reliably prefer the schedule that works worse, then offering spacing as an option will not be enough, because most people will switch it off. Tools should schedule reviews by default and explain briefly why the harder feeling is a good sign. Courses could also stop testing only at the end of each unit, since those tests reward the wrong habit.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text: The sample was small and drawn from two community centres in one city, so it may not represent adult learners in general. The study used a single language and a single list of words, and the schedule parameters were fixed rather than adapted to each learner. It also measured recall only, not whether participants could use the words in conversation, which is what most of them wanted.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text: A natural next step is an adaptive schedule that lengthens gaps only after a successful recall, compared against the fixed expanding schedule used here. It would also be worth testing whether telling learners about the prediction gap changes the schedules they choose for themselves when given the freedom to decide.

title: Spaced Review and Vocabulary Retention in Adult Language Learners
chunk_text: Arranging the same amount of review differently in time made a large difference to what adult learners still knew two months later, and no difference at all on a test at the end of study. The benefit was strongest for abstract words, and learners consistently believed the less effective schedule was working better. Anyone designing a course or a study tool for adults should build spacing in by default and measure success well after the learning has ended.

Arranging the same amount of review differently in time made a large difference to what adult learners still knew two months later, and no difference at all on a test at the end of study. The benefit was strongest for abstract words, and learners consistently believed the less effective schedule was working better. Anyone designing a course or a study tool for adults should build spacing in by default and measure success well after the learning has ended.
